title: Resilience & Backpressure
subtitle: Bound waiting, retries, concurrency, and admitted work so one failure cannot consume the whole system
objectives: Set end-to-end deadlines and retry budgets
Use circuit breakers and bulkheads to contain dependency failure
Propagate backpressure through queues and streams
Choose load shedding from request value and remaining capacity

exercises.title: A deadline bounds the total time and work spent on one request
exercises.body: Carry one end-to-end deadline through every dependency instead of granting each hop a fresh timeout. Each service subtracts time already spent, stops work that can no longer produce a useful response, and reserves enough time to return or recover.
exercises.note: Timeouts bound waiting at one hop; a propagated deadline protects the complete request budget.

exercises.prompt: Three nested service layers each make up to three attempts total for a failing downstream call. One user request can trigger `3 × 3 × 3 = 27` database attempts. Restrict retries to one owner and one shared budget.
choices: Retry faster at every layer
Let one layer retry with a bounded budget and jitter
Remove every timeout
choiceFeedback: Layered retries multiply attempts and synchronize load against the failing dependency.
One retry owner bounds amplification and jitter reduces synchronized retry waves.
Without timeouts, stuck attempts retain resources indefinitely.
exercises.beforeStatus: ONE REQUEST · up to 27 database attempts
exercises.afterStatus: ONE REQUEST · at most 2 database attempts within deadline
exercises.why: Retries consume dependency capacity and must fit inside the request deadline. One retry owner, capped attempts, exponential backoff, and jitter prevent multiplicative and synchronized retry load; non-idempotent work also needs retry-safe semantics.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Three nested service layers each make up to three attempts total for a failing downstream call. One user request can trigger `3 × 3 × 3 = 27` database attempts. Restrict retries to one owner and one shared budget. Place Retry owner, Database. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Request → Retry owner; Retry owner → Database. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Retries consume dependency capacity and must fit inside the request deadline. One retry owner, capped attempts, exponential backoff, and jitter prevent multiplicative and synchronized retry load; non-idempotent work also needs retry-safe semantics.

exercises.prompt: When is an automatic retry defensible? Select all.
choices: The failure is plausibly transient
The operation is idempotent or protected by an idempotency key
The remaining deadline can contain another attempt
The dependency is already overloaded and every caller retries immediately
exercises.why: A retry needs a transient failure hypothesis, safe repeated effects, and enough remaining time. Immediate fleet-wide retries during overload increase the failure rather than recovering from it.

steps: Attempt the operation with the propagated deadline
Classify the failure as retryable or terminal
Check remaining time and retry budget
Wait using capped backoff with jitter
Retry with the same operation identity
exercises.why: Classification prevents retrying permanent errors, the budget bounds work, jitter spreads callers over time, and the same identity preserves one intended effect across attempts.

exercises.title: Retries form a positive-feedback loop during overload
exercises.body: Slowness causes timeouts; timeouts cause retries; retries add work and create more slowness. A retry budget caps extra attempts relative to original traffic, while exponential backoff and jitter prevent synchronized return waves.
exercises.note: Retries spend remaining capacity, so they must be rarer as the dependency becomes less healthy.

exercises.prompt: A dependency receives 8,000 original ops/sec. Every timeout would retry once; capacity is 10,000 attempts/sec. Drag the *smallest* potential-retry share blocked by the retry budget.
exercises.why: Retrying every operation doubles load to 16,000 attempts/sec. Blocking 75% of retries permits 2,000 retries and reaches the 10,000 limit. The safer operating point keeps additional headroom for recovery.

exercises.title: A circuit breaker stops sending normal traffic to a dependency that is already failing
exercises.body: A breaker records recent outcomes. After a configured failure threshold it opens and fails calls quickly, then permits limited probes after a delay. Successful probes close it; failed probes preserve isolation while the dependency recovers.
exercises.note: A breaker protects caller resources and dependency recovery. It does not repair the dependency or define the fallback response.

exercises.prompt: Thumbnail generation occupies all 100 worker threads while its provider is stalled, so payment receipts cannot run. Isolate the two workloads.
choices: Double every timeout
Give thumbnails and receipts separate worker pools and queues
Put both workloads in one larger unbounded queue
choiceFeedback: Longer waits retain the shared threads for more time.
Separate pools contain thumbnail saturation and preserve receipt capacity.
An unbounded shared queue delays both workloads and can exhaust memory.
exercises.beforeStatus: SHARED POOL · 100/100 threads blocked · receipts unavailable
exercises.result: One dependency failure no longer consumes unrelated capacity
exercises.why: Bulkheads reserve independent concurrency and queue capacity for workloads with different dependencies or importance. Pool sizes and rejection behavior must be explicit so isolation does not become hidden underutilization.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Thumbnail generation occupies all 100 worker threads while its provider is stalled, so payment receipts cannot run. Isolate the two workloads. Place Separate limits. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Thumbnail pool → Separate limits; Receipt pool → Separate limits. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Bulkheads reserve independent concurrency and queue capacity for workloads with different dependencies or importance. Pool sizes and rejection behavior must be explicit so isolation does not become hidden underutilization.

exercises.prompt: Match each resilience control to the resource it bounds.

pairs.right: Calls admitted to a failing dependency

exercises.why: Deadlines bound time, bulkheads partition caller capacity, and circuit breakers suppress calls during observed failure. The controls solve different propagation paths and are commonly combined.

exercises.prompt: A circuit is open. What should a half-open state do?
choices: Send the full backlog immediately
Allow a limited number of probe requests
Delete all queued data
Disable monitoring
exercises.why: Limited probes test whether the dependency has recovered without restoring full load. Their success or failure drives the transition back to closed or open state.

lessons.title: Shed optional work before the dependency collapses

exercises.title: Load shedding preserves a smaller service instead of losing the whole service
exercises.body: When a dependency handles 9,000 operations/sec but incoming work reaches 15,000, optional requests must be rejected, degraded, or deferred before consuming dependency capacity. Priorities decide which work survives; random failure after saturation protects nobody.
exercises.note: Shedding is a product decision: checkout may survive while recommendations disappear.

exercises.prompt: Incoming work is 15,000 ops/sec and the dependency handles 9,000. Drag the *smallest* low-priority share to shed before the dependency.
exercises.why: Shedding 40% removes 6,000 optional operations and leaves 9,000 for the dependency. The protected workload must be selected before saturation; otherwise queueing and retries can consume the same capacity intended for critical work.

exercises.title: Backpressure makes a fast producer respond to a slower consumer
exercises.body: When arrival rate exceeds processing rate, a bounded system must slow producers, reject work, degrade optional features, or spill to a durable buffer with a defined limit. An unbounded queue converts overload into growing latency and memory use.
exercises.note: Backpressure must cross every asynchronous boundary; hiding it inside one queue only delays where overload becomes visible.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Backpressure makes a fast producer respond to a slower consumer
exercises.why: When arrival rate exceeds processing rate, a bounded system must slow producers, reject work, degrade optional features, or spill to a durable buffer with a defined limit. An unbounded queue converts overload into growing latency and memory use. Backpressure must cross every asynchronous boundary; hiding it inside one queue only delays where overload becomes visible.

exercises.prompt: Tap the component that first requires an overload policy.
exercises.why: The consumer drains 8,000 events/s while 10,000 arrive, so backlog grows by 2,000 each second. A bounded queue buys time but cannot remove the sustained rate mismatch.

exercises.prompt: Which overload responses preserve the core checkout path? Select all.
choices: Reject low-priority recommendations
Bound concurrent checkout work
Return a retryable overload response before expensive work
Accept every request into an unbounded in-memory queue
exercises.why: Dropping optional work, bounding concurrency, and rejecting early preserve capacity for core operations. An unbounded queue increases latency and memory consumption until the process fails.

exercises.prompt: Analytics events may be delayed for ten minutes but must not exhaust API memory. Choose the buffering emphasis.
exercises.rightLabel: Bounded durable queue with producer throttling
exercises.why: A bounded durable queue absorbs temporary delay without tying retention to one process's memory. When its limit is reached, producer throttling or explicit shedding keeps resource use finite.

exercises.prompt: A recommendations dependency slows down, and checkout threads wait indefinitely for it. Which change protects checkout first?
choices: A larger recommendation payload
One global queue with no bound
A short deadline and fallback that omits recommendations
Unlimited retries
exercises.why: Recommendations are optional to checkout. A deadline bounds occupied resources and a fallback preserves the critical path instead of allowing one slow dependency to exhaust it.
